title: Rebuilding a monolith segment as an event-driven microservice
question: Tell me about a time you had to align conflicting stakeholders.

situation: Because of my domain expertise, I was loaned for a year to a specialised cloud engineering team, to move a core segment of the legacy financial application into a cloud-native microservices architecture.
task: The goal was to port legacy logic into a new stack — Java, Kafka, JPA, Docker. But the legacy application was tightly coupled, so we had to re-architect the service from scratch, from a blend of historical specifications and entirely new cloud requirements.
action: Cross-functional alignment: I was the technical bridge between product owners, UX designers and engineering. When requirements conflicted — UX asking for late specification changes, or technical writers misreading legacy constraints — I ran alignment meetings to establish a single source of truth.

Modern engineering: I implemented standard JPA data layers and orchestrated event-driven communication with Apache Kafka. Just as importantly, I introduced comprehensive automated unit and integration testing.
result: Delivered the cloud-native microservice on schedule, and established a blueprint for how the company could systematically break its monolith into event-driven services.

challenge: Managing fragmented documentation and conflicting stakeholder requirements, particularly where the official requirements lacked the historical and technical context behind them.
hardestBug: An asynchronous data integrity issue during Kafka event replays. When certain business events were squashed by compaction during a replay, it triggered foreign key violations on linked entity deletions. I resolved it by refactoring the event-handling lifecycle and auditing data integrity at the application level during replays.
learned: Stakeholder management and conflict resolution, and how to communicate technical limitations to non-technical teams by aligning on shared project goals rather than on the constraint itself.
enjoyed: The move to modern practice — Docker, Kafka event streams, JPA, and the confidence that automated integration testing gives you.
